posts.title: All-WNBA: One Angel Reese Swap, Two Valkyries Cases
posts.dek: Angel Reese made Second Team, but her season belongs in the First Team debate. Golden State’s empty All-WNBA row leaves two more names worth talking about.
posts.imageAlt: Olivia Miles of the Minnesota Lynx handling the ball during a game.
posts.storyImageCaption: Olivia Miles in action for Minnesota. Photo: Getty Images / WNBA.
storyLead: Angel Reese made the 2026 All-WNBA Second Team. Calling her snubbed from All-WNBA misses the real question: after Defensive Player of the Year, a league-best 12.1 rebounds per game and a record 32 double-doubles, should she have been in the First Team five?

My answer is yes. I’d move Reese into the First Team and slide Breanna Stewart to the Second. I’d also give Golden State’s Gabby Williams the last Second Team spot. Veronica Burton makes a strong case right behind her.

sections.title: The top five made sense. The debate starts after that.
paragraphs: The official First Team—A’ja Wilson, Olivia Miles, Kelsey Mitchell, Caitlin Clark and Breanna Stewart—matches the five highest finishers in MVP voting. The ballot has a clear spine: Wilson’s fifth MVP, Miles’ unanimous Rookie of the Year season, Mitchell’s record scoring, Clark’s scoring and playmaking, and Stewart’s all-around production.

But All-WNBA is a second award with a second team. It can recognize a wider range of season-long impact than the MVP race. A neat match between the two ballots does not mean every difficult choice has been settled.

sections.title: Angel was selected. The question is where.
paragraphs: Reese averaged 16.4 points, 12.1 rebounds, 2.8 assists and 1.8 steals. She led the league in rebounding, set the WNBA single-season double-double record with 32, passed 500 rebounds, and became the first player in Atlanta Dream history to win Defensive Player of the Year.

That is more than a specialist’s résumé. Reese carried a large share of Atlanta’s scoring, ended possessions on the glass and earned the league’s top defensive honor. The Second Team nod is deserved. The First Team case is real.

sections.title: My move: Reese up, Stewart down one row
paragraphs: If I’m choosing five players for the biggest individual seasons, I put Reese ahead of Stewart. The difference is narrow, and Stewart has a strong counter: 20.8 points, 8.3 rebounds and 3.3 assists per game, a top-five finish in win shares, and a place in the top ten in scoring, rebounding and blocks. She was still one of the league’s best players.

But the First Team should leave room for a season that changed the math on both ends. Reese’s record rebounding, 32 double-doubles and Defensive Player of the Year honor are the kind of season that should break through the familiar scoring hierarchy. Stewart stays All-WNBA on my ballot—she just moves to Second.

sections.title: The other four stay put
paragraphs: Wilson led the league with 26.2 points per game and 9.43 win shares. Mitchell scored 24.7 per game and set the single-season points record. Clark finished among the top three in both points and assists, creating 41.2 points per game. Miles averaged 19.8 points and 6.0 assists, won Rookie of the Year unanimously, and helped lead Minnesota to the league’s best record.
I can make an Angel Reese argument without pretending those seasons were ordinary. They weren’t.

sections.title: Second Team is not a consolation plate
paragraphs: Paige Bueckers paired 20.9 points with 5.9 assists and shot 51.2 percent from the field, 41 percent from three and 87.1 percent at the line. Jackie Young posted 18.9 points and 6.8 assists while shooting nearly 49 percent. Rhyne Howard averaged 17.7 points, led the league in steals and finished second in three-pointers.

Shakira Austin brought 17 points, 9.5 rebounds and 20 double-doubles. She belongs in this conversation even though I’d give the last Second Team spot to Williams. The gap between those cases is small; the gap between either player and an ordinary season is not.

sections.title: Golden State has two names worth a second look
paragraphs: The Valkyries went 32–12, finished second in the standings and reached the Finals without an All-WNBA selection. The Finals run cannot be used to rewrite a regular-season award, but that regular season deserves more than a shrug.

Williams is my Valkyries pick. She averaged 14.4 points and 1.6 steals, led Golden State in scoring, made the All-Defensive First Team and finished runner-up for Defensive Player of the Year. On my alternate ballot, I’d take her over Austin for the final Second Team spot. Austin’s 17 points and 9.5 rebounds make that a real cut, not an easy one.

Burton also deserves a mention. She averaged 12.2 points and 5.7 assists, made All-Defensive Second Team, and finished with 7.55 win shares—second in the league only to Wilson. Her scoring was lower than the other honorees, but her two-way value and effect on winning were hard to miss.
Angel Reese wasn’t left off the list. My snub call is about her placement. For the Valkyries, Williams is the clearest All-WNBA omission, with Burton close behind.

posts.title: The $700 Million Sparks Question: What Is the Team Actually Worth?
posts.dek: A report says Mark Walter is seeking more than $700 million for the Sparks and their planned practice facility. That is an asking price for a package, not a confirmed valuation of the team alone.
storyLead: More than $700 million is the number attached to the Los Angeles Sparks this week. Bloomberg reporting, carried by the Los Angeles Times, says controlling owner Mark Walter is seeking that amount for the franchise and its related practice facility.

That figure is not a completed sale, a confirmed offer, or a stand-alone price for the team. The package includes a major facility project, so the headline number needs a label before anyone calls it the Sparks’ valuation.

franchiseValueDashboard.title: Three numbers. Three different measures.
franchiseValueDashboard.intro: An asking price, a third-party estimate and a completed transaction are not interchangeable.
franchiseValueDashboard.summaryLabel: reported ask for the Sparks + practice facility
franchiseValueDashboard.summaryNote: The report describes a sale effort, not a completed deal.

cards.label: Reported package asking price
cards.note: Sparks franchise plus its related El Segundo practice facility, according to Bloomberg reporting.

cards.label: Sportico franchise estimate
cards.note: A team-only estimate cited by the Los Angeles Times; published in April 2026.

cards.label: Reported Sun transaction
cards.note: The Connecticut Sun sale price, cited as the previous WNBA record.

franchiseValueDashboard.methodology: Different scope and timing: the reported $700M+ ask bundles the team and facility; $400M is an estimate of the franchise; $300M is a reported sale price. They are context, not direct comparables.

sections.title: What the report actually says
paragraphs: Bloomberg’s report says Walter is seeking more than $700 million for the Sparks and a related practice facility. The Los Angeles Times, which published the report, says the package would be the largest WNBA franchise sale to date if a deal reached that level.
No buyer or completed agreement is named in the report. A seller’s asking price can start a conversation; it does not tell us what a buyer will pay or what the league will approve.

sections.title: The facility is a real part of the package
paragraphs: The Sparks announced a $150 million headquarters and practice facility in El Segundo, with an opening planned before the 2027 season. The project adds dedicated training and performance space to the assets being discussed.
Construction cost is not the same as market value. The published report does not break out how much of the asking price is attributed to the team, the facility, or other deal terms.

sections.title: The comparison needs a warning label
paragraphs: The Los Angeles Times cites Sportico’s April 2026 estimate of $400 million for the Sparks franchise. It also cites the $300 million reported price for the Connecticut Sun as the previous WNBA sale record.

Those figures help explain why the report is striking, but they measure different things. The $700 million-plus figure includes the facility; the $400 million estimate is for the team; and the Sun number reflects a separate transaction. We should not present them as a clean three-team valuation chart.

sections.title: Why this matters beyond Los Angeles
paragraphs: The Sparks are an original WNBA franchise in one of the country’s largest sports markets, and their new facility represents a substantial long-term investment. At the same time, the team has missed the playoffs for six straight seasons. A buyer would be weighing the brand and market against the work still needed on the court.

The league reported more than 90 million unique viewers across national networks during the 2026 regular season. That is meaningful growth context, but it is a league-wide audience figure, not proof of what the Sparks are worth.

sections.title: What would make the number real?
paragraphs: The next receipts would be a named buyer, a reported or approved transaction price, and clarity about what the deal includes: the team, the facility, any retained ownership interests, and related obligations. Until then, $700 million-plus is a reported asking price for a package—not a confirmed sale price.
We will update the board if the Sparks, Walter, a buyer, or the WNBA confirms new terms.

foodSegment.title: A headline has a number. A sale has terms.
foodSegment.script: The $700M question is worth watching. The answer depends on what changes hands, who buys it, and what the league approves.

posts.title: The Fever’s Front-Office Reset: What Comes Next for Cox, White and Kelsey?
posts.dek: Kelly Krauskopf’s step-down is official. The Athletic reports the Fever will part ways with COO and GM Amber Cox, though the team has not confirmed that report. With no successors named, Stephanie White’s future and Kelsey Mitchell’s free agency now sit inside a larger leadership reset.
posts.imageAlt: Kelly Krauskopf speaks at a press conference after returning to the Indiana Fever as president.
posts.storyImageCaption: Kelly Krauskopf at her 2024 return press conference. Photo: Indiana Fever / WNBA.
storyLead: The Indiana Fever announced on October 23 that Kelly Krauskopf will step down as team president. The official statement did not name a successor or say where Krauskopf will go next.

Separately, The Athletic reported that Indiana plans to fire COO and general manager Amber Cox. The Fever’s announcement addressed Krauskopf’s departure; it did not confirm Cox’s reported exit. The Athletic also reported Krauskopf had made her decision before the 2026 regular season ended, so the two developments should not be treated as one cause-and-effect move.

No replacement has been announced. Our early forecast: ownership needs to define who leads basketball operations before the next free-agency window. That decision now shapes the coaching review and the pitch to unrestricted free agent Kelsey Mitchell.

frontOfficeForecast.title: Four questions, four calls
frontOfficeForecast.dek: One departure is confirmed; one is reported. Forecasts are labeled and kept separate from team announcements.

cards.name: Successors not named
cards.forecast: Our low-confidence call is that ownership names a president with clear basketball authority, then lets that leader shape the GM hire. That gives the next roster decision-maker a defined mandate. No credible front-runner has been reported, so we are not putting a name on the board.

cards.name: No next role reported
cards.status: The Athletic reports Indiana will part ways
cards.forecast: Cox’s career spans WNBA team operations and senior roles across professional sports. A return to a team or league operations post is plausible, but no destination or hiring interest has been reported. A specific team guess would be speculation without evidence.

cards.name: Stephanie White
cards.status: One more season remains our lean
cards.forecast: White said she wants to return, and Indiana won 28 regular-season games before losing its first-round series 1–2. We lean toward keeping her for 2027, but the new president and basketball lead may want to choose their own coach. The leadership change lowers our confidence.

cards.name: Kelsey Mitchell
cards.forecast: A fresh leadership group could reset the relationship, but Mitchell needs a clear role and a credible plan to build a playoff defense. She has said she will put her own needs first. Indiana can make a competitive offer; it cannot count on core designation to control her decision.

frontOfficeForecast.note: Forecasts are editorial judgment, not reporting about private negotiations. The Fever have not announced a new president, general manager, coach decision, or contract offer to Mitchell.

sections.title: Two developments, two different levels of confirmation
paragraphs: The Fever’s October 23 statement confirms that Kelly Krauskopf will step down as team president after nearly three decades with Pacers Sports & Entertainment. It does not identify a successor or explain the decision.

The Athletic separately reports that Indiana will fire Amber Cox, who held the combined COO and general-manager roles. That report is based on multiple sources; the Fever had not confirmed it in the statement about Krauskopf when this update was prepared. The Athletic also says Krauskopf’s decision came before the end of the regular season. The timing puts both leadership questions in front of the franchise at once, but it does not establish that the decisions were connected.

sections.title: Who leads basketball operations next?
paragraphs: There is no public candidate list. Our forecast is structural rather than a name prediction: ownership hires or designates the person who will lead the Fever as a whole, then clearly assigns that leader responsibility for the general-manager search and roster decisions.

An internal promotion is possible, but we do not have a verified report identifying a front-runner. We lean toward a broader search because the president and GM roles now need clear lines of accountability, and the franchise cannot let the coaching decision and Mitchell’s free agency drift without an owner.

Our early call: the Fever bring in a president with basketball authority and have that executive select or formally empower a GM. Confidence is low. The next announcement, not fan speculation, will tell us whether Indiana chooses continuity or a full reset.

sections.title: What could be next for Amber Cox?
paragraphs: No next job has been reported. Cox has worked in senior team and league-facing roles across women’s basketball and professional sports, including the Phoenix Mercury, Connecticut Sun, Dallas Wings and Indiana Fever.

That experience makes another team or league operations role plausible. A return to a broader COO or president’s post is one possible lane; taking time before choosing the next role is another. There is no evidence tying her to a particular franchise, so we will not turn a résumé-based possibility into a destination rumor.

sections.title: Could Steph get one more year?
paragraphs: White has a case to return. Indiana finished 28–16, and White was named WNBA Coach of the Month for July. The Fever then lost their first-round series to Las Vegas 1–2, making playoff defense and late-game execution the next tests.

White said after the season that she felt supported and hoped to continue, while acknowledging the decision belongs to the organization. Our lean is still to bring her back for 2027. A coach who delivered 28 wins deserves a serious review, and continuity could help a new front office settle the roster.

That is now a lower-confidence call. A new president or GM may want to hire a coach they selected, and the defensive problems will be part of that discussion. White’s job has not been announced as safe or in jeopardy.

sections.title: Will the reset be enough to keep Kelsey Mitchell?
paragraphs: Mitchell’s 2026 season made the question impossible to postpone. She averaged 24.7 points per game and set Indiana’s single-season scoring record with 1,086 points. After nine seasons with the Fever, she is entering unrestricted free agency in 2027.

Mitchell has said she intends to be selfish about what she needs from her next decision. The reported leadership change gives Indiana a chance to make a new pitch, but it also means the people selling that pitch may not yet be in place. A familiar jersey and a strong offer are not the same thing as a convincing basketball plan.

The Fever’s 2026 supermax agreement does not automatically settle her next contract. Indiana cannot rely on another core designation to keep her from choosing among teams. The new basketball lead will need to show Mitchell her role beside Caitlin Clark and Aliyah Boston, how the roster will improve its playoff defense, and who is accountable for that plan.

Our current read remains a slight lean toward Mitchell exploring a move. A new leadership team could change that answer if it arrives quickly with a clear role, a credible roster plan, and the freedom to make a competitive offer. The reset alone will not keep her; what the reset builds might.

sections.title: The decision that reaches beyond one contract
paragraphs: The question is larger than whether Indiana keeps one star or one coach. The Fever have to decide who owns the basketball plan, who makes the case to Mitchell, and what kind of team they are building around Clark and Boston.

Our best forecast today: Krauskopf’s next destination remains unknown, Cox may return to team or league operations after a pause, Indiana is more likely than not to keep White for another season, and Mitchell is the swing decision. Each call is low confidence until the Fever name their leadership and put a real 2027 plan on the table.

foodSegment.title: What would convince Kelsey Mitchell to stay?
foodSegment.script: Would a new front office be enough, or does Indiana need to show Kelsey Mitchell a specific plan for the roster, defense and her role beside Caitlin Clark and Aliyah Boston?

posts.title: From $15K to $270K: WNBA Minimum Pay Through the Years
posts.dek: The lowest standard full-season minimum was $15,000. Trace the pay milestones, the 2026 CBA jump and the league growth behind the new numbers.
storyLead: The WNBA’s lowest standard full-season minimum base salary was $15,000 in its early seasons. For 2026, the new collective bargaining agreement sets the minimum between $270,000 and $300,000, depending on service time. That is an 18-fold rise at the low end, in dollars of the day.
The climb came in labor-deal steps, not one smooth annual curve. The timeline tracks the lowest salary tier and keeps base pay separate from the Finals bonuses shown below.

sections.title: The least was $15,000
paragraphs: That is the league’s early standard minimum base salary. It is not an estimate of what every player earned. The first player labor agreement raised the minimum in 1999 to $25,000 for rookies and $30,000 for veterans. Years of service have shaped the minimum ever since.
The timeline shows selected salary floors, not every season. It also uses nominal dollars: $15,000 in 1997 did not buy what $15,000 buys today.

sections.title: The steepest jump arrived with a new labor deal
paragraphs: The 2020 agreement moved the inexperienced-player minimum to $57,000 and the experienced-player minimum to $68,000. By 2025, the lower tier had reached $66,079, with the veteran tier at $78,831.
Then the 2026 agreement reset the scale. Its $270,000 low-end minimum is about 4.1 times the 2025 low end, a roughly 309% increase in one season. The $300,000 figure applies to higher service tiers.

sections.title: The league is growing around the pay scale
paragraphs: The 2026 season drew a record 3.8 million fans across 330 regular-season games. Average attendance was 11,474 per game, 21% above the previous record; the league also reported more than 90 million unique viewers and 4 billion social views, up 28% from 2025.

The new CBA lifted the team salary cap from $1.5 million in 2025 to $7 million in 2026 and added a comprehensive revenue-sharing model. The league says future caps will adjust with team and league revenue growth. That is a negotiated way for player compensation to move with the business. That does not mean every new fan automatically increases a player’s paycheck.

sections.title: Finals bonuses are a separate win
paragraphs: Finals bonuses climbed sharply too: a player on the 2025 championship team received $22,908, compared with $60,000 under the 2026 schedule. The Finals MVP bonus rose from $5,000 to $30,000, while the runner-up bonus moved from $8,521 to $20,000.
These are per-player postseason bonuses, on top of base salary. They should not be read as annual pay.

foodSegment.title: The floor changed; the fight built the ladder
foodSegment.script: From $15K at the start to a $270K minimum in 2026: a dramatic 18× jump in nominal dollars, with the next chapter tied to how the league’s revenue grows.

posts.title: The Fifth Spot Has Four Names
posts.dek: The all-time graphic stops after A’ja Wilson and the three-time winners. The next place is a four-way tie, with Candace Parker among the names to add.
posts.imageAlt: Candace Parker poses with the WNBA MVP and Rookie of the Year awards before the 2008 Finals

storyLead: A’ja Wilson’s fifth regular-season MVP, announced October 8, puts her alone atop the WNBA count. The graphic names Wilson and the three-time winners Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson. Add the next place and the board needs four names: Cynthia Cooper, Candace Parker, Elena Delle Donne and Breanna Stewart each won twice.

Candace is a natural fifth face to add to a four-person graphic, but she is not the only player in fifth place. In standard ranking, the three-time winners tie for second and the four two-time winners tie for fifth. The sortable board below keeps that tie visible.

sections.title: The tie changes the fifth slot
paragraphs: The WNBA’s official season-by-season list confirms five for Wilson; three apiece for Swoopes, Leslie and Jackson; and two each for Cooper, Parker, Delle Donne and Stewart. That creates a four-player tie for fifth by award count. A fifth portrait can start the next row, but a complete history needs all four.

Parker’s résumé makes her an especially fitting addition. She earned MVP and Rookie of the Year in 2008, then added her second MVP in 2013. Cooper’s two came in consecutive seasons at the league’s start; Delle Donne won with Chicago and Washington; Stewart’s came with Seattle and New York.

sections.title: MVP count is one lens, not a GOAT ballot
paragraphs: This board counts regular-season MVP awards. It does not add Finals MVPs, titles, All-WNBA selections or career totals. Those are different questions, and combining them would turn a clean record into a subjective score.

posts.title: Six Rookies, Five Spots, and the Long Game
posts.dek: A tied fifth place made six 2026 AP All-Rookie honorees. Put their season in context, then rank the most accomplished All-Rookie classes and find the future stars the ballot missed.
posts.imageAlt: Olivia Miles of the Minnesota Lynx handling the ball during a game

storyLead: A tie for fifth expanded the 2026 AP All-Rookie Team to six honorees: Pauline Astier, Azzi Fudd, Flau’jae Johnson, Olivia Miles, Kiki Rice and Sydney Taylor. Miles was the unanimous Rookie of the Year, and her 790 points set a WNBA rookie scoring record. One team, six different paths to recognition.

A rookie team is a snapshot of a season. A historical ranking is a look backward at what careers became. Keep those questions separate: the first dashboard compares this class on its rookie-year production, while the history board ranks older teams on the careers that followed.

sections.title: One class, six different jobs
paragraphs: The AP’s sixth selection is not a second-tier footnote. A tie for fifth expands a five-place honor to six. It also shows the voting problem: rookies do not enter identical situations. A guard asked to create every night has a different statistical profile from a shooter, a reserve organizer or a wing learning a veteran team’s system.

Miles’ 19.8 points and 6.0 assists make the highest-volume case. Fudd’s 39.7% from three is the cleanest spacing signal in this group. Johnson pairs 14.9 points with 4.8 rebounds. Taylor’s 13.6 points and two late game-winners say something about her shot creation and timing. Astier’s 3.3 assists and efficient scoring fit a different kind of need. Rice’s 12.9 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.5 assists show why a short season can still leave a mark.

Those numbers do not settle who has the best career ahead. They describe the work each player did in this season, in this role. A useful rookie award can honor that without pretending to be a draft redo.

sections.title: How the historical top ten got its shape
paragraphs: The board is deliberately retrospective. The 2008 team gets the top spot on the strength of Parker and Fowles together. The 2018 class owns the highest peak because of Wilson. The 2006 five rises when the question is depth; its three headliners carried long, decorated careers. Press “Peak star” or “Class depth” and those trade-offs become visible instead of hiding inside one number.

2019 and 2014 rank well because their strength is spread across several proven careers. 2013 is a top-three peak class. 2016 is more complicated: Stewart makes the official five exceptional, but the absent Jonquel Jones and Kahleah Copper eventually won league MVP and Finals MVP awards. The snub file puts that counterfactual in view without quietly changing the official team.

This is an editorial ranking with a defined window, not a claim that older players are better. Classes from 2020 onward get a watchlist treatment because their career records are still being written. Time is part of the comparison.

sections.title: The Food for Thought question
paragraphs: If you could replay the rookie ballot with only that season’s evidence, which borderline choice would you change? Now ask the harder version: if you knew the whole career, would your answer change? The first question is about judging a season fairly. The second is about how poorly one early label can measure the distance a player still has to travel.

Jonquel Jones and Kahleah Copper make the 2016 question almost unfair in hindsight. Their rookie years were quiet; their later peaks were not. All-Rookie is a strong note on the opening chapter. It is not the ending.

foodSegment.title: One vote is a snapshot
foodSegment.script: The 2026 rookie class gave us six honest cases for five spots. Career hindsight gives us another lesson: a rookie list can tell you who stood out first. It cannot tell you how far the player will go.

posts.title: Preseason Hype Has Homework: Who Really Looks Ready for 2026–27?
posts.dek: South Carolina leads ESPN’s Top 25, JuJu returns to USC, and UCLA starts at No. 13. The real debate is what each contender still has to prove.
posts.imageAlt: Joyce Edwards drives against Sarah Strong

sections.title: October crowns do not come with nets
paragraphs: Preseason rankings are basketball’s seating chart. They tell us who gets the good table before anybody has served the food. ESPN’s October 13 list puts South Carolina, UConn and USC in the first three seats. That is a useful starting point. It is also an invitation to ask what would make those choices look smart in March.

Our question is simple: are we ranking a program’s reputation, a roster’s ceiling, or the team we expect to trust when a close game turns ugly? Those can be three different answers. A roster can win the introduction and still need months to learn how to win the possession.
The ranks below belong to ESPN, not an AP poll and not a We Know the W score. The watch questions and verdicts are our editorial analysis. Nobody has earned a 2026–27 regular-season résumé yet.

sections.title: South Carolina: being the favorite means showing your work
paragraphs: South Carolina at No. 1 is defensible. It should also invite the toughest examination. Our test for Dawn Staley’s team is the quality of its half-court possessions: who organizes the offense, who gets the ball to the right spot, and who creates a good shot after the first option disappears?

A favorite does not need to look flawless in November. It needs workable answers. Watch late-clock decisions, spacing around the paint, and whether the same action can produce multiple reads instead of one predictable finish. Defensive pressure can create easy points; a championship opponent will try to take those away.
The W verdict: keep South Carolina in the first tier. Make it earn separation through possession quality. The logo is an introduction; the execution is the argument.

sections.title: UConn: Sarah Strong is the foundation, not the entire building
paragraphs: UConn enters with Sarah Strong, the reigning national player of the year and unanimous BIG EAST preseason player of the year. KK Arnold and Blanca Quiñonez also earned unanimous preseason all-conference selections. Those are real reasons to expect a contender, confirmed by the program’s October 1 announcement.

Our film question is what happens when opponents load up on Strong. Can the next receiver attack the advantage before the defense resets? Can a second creator rescue a possession without turning it into a difficult solo shot? The supporting cast matters most when an opponent has spent a week designing a plan for the star.

For WNBA scouting, Strong’s value is not confined to scoring. Track the speed of her reads, defensive coverage changes, and decisions against help. A prospect who makes the right play when the easiest play is unavailable is telling us something useful.

sections.title: USC: JuJu is back. The chemistry still has to arrive
paragraphs: USC confirms JuJu Watkins is returning after missing 2025–26 through injury. Both conference coaches and media named her Big Ten preseason player of the year. Jazzy Davidson joins her on the preseason all-conference teams after leading USC in points, rebounds, assists, steals and blocks last season.

That makes No. 3 understandable. It does not make cohesion automatic. A returning star and an established young creator need shared timing: when to initiate, when to cut, when to clear a side, and when to turn a touch into an advantage for somebody else.

We should judge Watkins’ return through basketball evidence rather than demanding a highlight reel immediately. Watch how the offense functions across multiple games, how responsibilities are distributed, and how the group responds to physical defense. A preseason honor is recognition, not a medical clearance or a guarantee about workload.

The W verdict: USC has an exciting ceiling. The first useful question is whether its talented players can make one another easier to guard less often. Talent gathers attention. Connected talent gathers wins.

sections.title: UCLA at 13: disrespect, or a different roster?
paragraphs: The defending champion starting at No. 13 is the obvious debate starter. UCLA’s own draft announcement supplies important context: six Bruins were selected in April, including five in the first round. That is a record-setting professional pipeline and a substantial amount of college production walking out the door.

Our read: the championship deserves full credit, while the new team deserves its own evaluation. It is reasonable to forecast uncertainty after that kind of departure. It is also reasonable to expect the coaching staff’s habits to carry over. Neither point settles what the next roster can accomplish.

Watch rebounding responsibilities, communication in transition, and which combinations remain functional when starters sit. Those details will tell us whether the Bruins are rebuilding continuity quickly. Calling every lower ranking disrespect skips the roster question; treating the title as irrelevant skips the coaching question.

sections.title: The rest of the table can change the conversation
paragraphs: Duke and Michigan complete ESPN’s top five. Louisville and Iowa sit sixth and seventh, ahead of LSU and Texas. North Carolina closes the top ten. Our challenge to that group is the same: identify the lineup you trust against a quality opponent, then show why it works.

The lower half deserves more than a drive-by. A team ranked in the teens can become a serious threat if its complementary pieces fit faster than expected. Conversely, a top-ten roster can spend the winter working through a problem everyone politely ignored in October.

For fans, the most useful early result is not always the biggest win. Watch what happens after a team’s preferred style gets disrupted. Can it defend without fouling, survive a cold shooting stretch, and finish a possession with a rebound? That is where preseason optimism starts becoming evidence.

sections.title: Who Got Next? Scout the job, not just the name
paragraphs: This season is also a new chapter in the WNBA pipeline. Watkins and Strong deserve attention, but scouting should not become a contest to see who can repeat the most famous names. Every prospect has to show skills that fit a professional role.

For a lead guard, watch decisions against pressure and the ability to manipulate help. For a wing, watch shooting preparation, closeout attacks and defensive assignments. For a big, watch screening angles, defensive positioning, finishing windows and passing when the paint is crowded.

College ranking, individual awards and draft position answer different questions. A freshman can reshape a contender without being part of the next draft. A veteran can be a compelling prospect on a team outside the top ten. Draft eligibility and declarations should be verified separately; being on our radar is not a declaration.
The Food for Thought takeaway: keep the rankings, keep the debate, and ask for the film. October gives us the hypothesis. The season gets to grade the homework.

posts.dek: Minnesota gave her two WNBA championships on the floor. Atlanta’s Finals berth puts Renee Montgomery back on the championship stage as a co-owner and vice president.

sections.title: Two titles, a new seat
paragraphs: Montgomery won WNBA titles with Minnesota in 2015 and 2017. She finished her 11-season playing career with Atlanta, sat out 2020 to focus on social reform, and joined the Dream’s ownership group in 2021. The team lists her as partner and vice president.

sections.title: A first with Atlanta
paragraphs: Atlanta clinched its first Finals berth since 2013 with an 85–83 win over New York on October 9. Lining up Montgomery’s Finals appearances with her ownership timeline makes her the first person in WNBA history to reach the series in both capacities: first with Minnesota as a player, now with Atlanta as a team owner.
The WNBA already marks her as the first former player to hold both team equity and an executive role. The 2026 berth adds a Finals milestone to that path.

sections.title: Why this belongs in the Finals story
paragraphs: The Dream’s players will decide the series on the floor; Montgomery is not suiting up. Her place in the story is different: a former player helps lead the franchise as it competes for its first championship.
That path from the court to ownership shows how a WNBA career can keep shaping the league after the final season ends.

posts.dek: The Valkyries have a Finals ticket and a reported $100 million revenue milestone. The scoreboard is only half the story.

sections.title: The violet receipts are in
paragraphs: According to Sportico’s October 7 report, covered by Field Level Media and Reuters on October 8, Golden State exceeded $100 million in annual revenue in 2026. The reporting identifies the Valkyries as the first women’s professional sports team to reach that mark.
That is revenue: money coming into the business before expenses. It does not establish $100 million in profit. A franchise valuation is a separate estimate of what the team is worth.

sections.title: Full buildings, then a Finals berth
paragraphs: Golden State sold out all 22 regular-season home games and finished 32–12. The second-year franchise then swept Las Vegas, clinching its first Finals appearance with an 87–77 overtime win on October 9.
Sportico also projected that a Finals run could lift gross revenue above $130 million. Golden State has now reached the series; that projection remains a projection, not a confirmed final total.

sections.title: Shak’s take
paragraphs: Ballhalla brought the noise. The balance sheet brought receipts. A packed arena and a winning roster make a strong business story, but one exceptional franchise is not a financial statement for the entire league.

The useful question now: how does that demand translate into lasting investment in players, staff and the fan experience? Golden State has shown what a market can support. The next chapter is what the organization does with it.

sections.title: Golden State skipped the waiting room
paragraphs: Golden State reached the 2026 WNBA Finals in its second season, sweeping defending champion Las Vegas with an 87–77 overtime win on October 9. The Valkyries are the first expansion franchise to reach the championship series that quickly.

Atlanta is the closest comparison. The Dream debuted in 2008 and reached the 2010 Finals in season three. Seattle arrived in 2000 and made its first Finals in 2004, season five. Detroit debuted in 1998 and reached—and won—the 2003 Finals in season six.

sections.title: The relocation receipt
paragraphs: Connecticut reached the 2004 Finals in its second season as the Sun. But that franchise began as the Orlando Miracle in 1999, making it season six of the franchise’s life. A new address does not reset the expansion clock.

sections.title: Another first: Reese gets there ahead of her draft peers
paragraphs: Angel Reese was the seventh selection in the 2024 WNBA Draft. With Atlanta’s October 9 clincher, she secured a Finals berth before the six players selected ahead of her: Caitlin Clark, Cameron Brink, Kamilla Cardoso, Rickea Jackson, Jacy Sheldon and Aaliyah Edwards.

That is a milestone in the 2024 class, not a verdict on six careers. Injuries, roster construction and team circumstances shape the route. Reese still earned her part: 22 points and nine rebounds in Atlanta’s 85–83 closeout in Brooklyn.

sections.title: Shak’s take
paragraphs: Atlanta brings the longer wait. Golden State brings the shortest runway. Neither franchise has won a WNBA championship.
The Valkyries unpacked their boxes and started shopping for a trophy case.

sections.title: A fifth award changes the WNBA record book
paragraphs: A’ja Wilson has won the 2026 Kia WNBA Most Valuable Player award, her fifth. Her first came in 2020, followed by 2022 and then three in a row from 2024 through 2026. That last stretch is a league first: no WNBA player had won three consecutive MVPs.

The award follows another historic regular season. Wilson averaged 26.2 points, 9.4 rebounds, 3.2 assists, 1.4 steals and 1.9 blocks in 41 games. She led the league in scoring, blocks and win shares. Her 26.2 points per game is the second-highest scoring average in WNBA history; only Wilson’s own 26.9 in 2024 is higher.
The numbers show why the season resisted a one-skill description. She carried an elite scoring load, controlled the glass and remained one of the league’s most disruptive rim protectors.

sections.title: The wider basketball comparison—and its limits
paragraphs: Five regular-season MVPs puts Wilson in rare company across professional basketball. It matches Michael Jordan’s five NBA MVPs and leaves her one behind Kareem Abdul-Jabbar’s NBA-record six.

That is a useful measure of how scarce the honor is, not proof that awards from different leagues or eras are interchangeable. The NBA and WNBA have distinct histories, schedules and voting contexts. The fair point is narrower: Wilson’s count now belongs beside the best-known MVP totals in the sport, while standing alone at the top of the WNBA.

sections.title: The full résumé reaches beyond the regular season
paragraphs: Wilson is also a three-time WNBA champion, a two-time Finals MVP and a three-time Defensive Player of the Year. She entered the league as its 2018 Rookie of the Year. The spread matters: her record includes sustained regular-season dominance, postseason performance, defense and team success.

Her international record adds another layer. USA Basketball lists Wilson as a two-time Olympic gold medalist, a two-time FIBA Women’s World Cup champion, the MVP of the 2022 World Cup and the MVP of the 2024 Paris Olympics. At South Carolina, she helped win the 2017 NCAA title and was named Final Four Most Outstanding Player.

sections.title: The record is settled; the season is still live
paragraphs: On October 7, Wilson scored a game-high 24 points and collected seven rebounds, but Las Vegas lost Game 2 of its semifinal series to Golden State, 83–81. The Aces now trail 0–2 in the best-of-five series and need a win at home to extend their title defense.

That tension is useful context for a legacy story. Individual awards recognize what a player did over a regular season; they do not decide what comes next. Wilson’s fifth MVP is already a record. The 2026 playoff chapter is still being written.

sections.title: Shak’s take
paragraphs: The fifth MVP is the headline, but the case for Wilson’s place among basketball’s most decorated players comes from the combination: a WNBA record, three straight MVPs, titles, Finals MVPs, defensive awards, Olympic and World Cup gold, and a college championship.
Wilson now owns more regular-season MVP awards than anyone in WNBA history. Her combination of individual honors and team success puts her among basketball’s most accomplished players.

posts.title: Down 0–2: Somebody Has to Be First
posts.imageAlt: Sue Bird drives past Yvonne Turner in Seattle against Phoenix during Game 5 on September 4, 2018
posts.storyImageCaption: Sue Bird drives past Phoenix’s Yvonne Turner during Game 5 in Seattle, September 4, 2018. Photo: Elaine Thompson/AP, via The Spokesman-Review.
posts.dek: Has a WNBA team ever won a playoff series after falling behind 0–2? As of October 8, 2026, no. Phoenix got closest in 2018. Then Masked Sue Bird happened.

sections.title: The short answer: not yet
paragraphs: No WNBA team has won a playoff series after losing its first two games, as of October 8, 2026. Coming back to tie a series is a different accomplishment from finishing the comeback. The 2018 Phoenix Mercury managed the first. Nobody has managed the second.
New York and Las Vegas now trail Atlanta and Golden State 0–2 in their best-of-five semifinals. Each needs three consecutive wins to advance. One win buys another game; it does not erase the deficit.

sections.title: Phoenix knocked. Bird changed the locks.
paragraphs: In 2018, Phoenix lost the first two semifinal games in Seattle, then won both games at home to force Game 5. The Mercury became the first WNBA team to push a series to a deciding fifth game after an 0–2 start.

Game 4 was its own escape act. Phoenix erased a 17-point deficit and won 86–84 on September 2. Brittney Griner scored the go-ahead basket with 14.1 seconds left, then helped deny Seattle’s final attempt.

Two nights later, Sue Bird shut the door. Wearing a protective mask after breaking her nose in Game 4, she scored 14 of her 22 points in the fourth quarter as Seattle won Game 5, 94–84. Phoenix reached the doorstep. Seattle kept the keys.

sections.title: Shak’s take
paragraphs: An 0–2 deficit is a history assignment with no completed answer key. The Liberty and Aces do not need to win three games on Friday. They need to win one, make the leaders pack for another, and repeat.
Impossible? The format allows it. Unprecedented? Absolutely. Somebody has to be first. Until then, Phoenix owns the closest call and Masked Sue owns the ending.

sections.title: From courtside to the cap table
paragraphs: Unrivaled announced on October 5 that actor, producer and entrepreneur Issa Rae has joined the league as an investor. The investment was made through the oversubscribed Series C round the league announced in August.

Rae said seeing Unrivaled firsthand last season convinced her that the league was building something special. Unrivaled also described this as her first league-wide investment, adding another entertainment and business name to an investor group already packed with athletes, coaches and cultural heavyweights.

sections.title: The number did not change. The signal did.
paragraphs: The $650 million valuation is not a fresh re-price caused by Rae's investment. That figure was set when Unrivaled announced the Series C on August 26. The round, led by Ten Pillars Sports Fund, surpassed its original $100 million target and was oversubscribed.

What changed today is the cap table. Rae joins an investor list that already includes Stephen Curry, Giannis Antetokounmpo, Coco Gauff, Billie Jean King, Alex Morgan, Dawn Staley, JuJu Watkins and others. Players remain the league's largest equity group, with Unrivaled valuing the player equity pool at nearly $200 million when the round was announced.

sections.title: Shak's bite
paragraphs: Celebrity money by itself is not a business model. But the kind of people choosing to buy in tells you what they think the business can become.

Issa Rae brings something different from another athlete investor: entertainment reach, brand-building experience and a track record of creating culture instead of simply attaching her name to it. Unrivaled has spent two seasons proving it can make basketball feel like an event. Now it is adding investors who know how to turn an event into a larger ecosystem.

sections.title: First, label the trophy correctly
paragraphs: These are the Associated Press awards, chosen by a 17-member media panel. They matter because the AP has kept the same core award slate since 2016 and its voters offer a clean, independent snapshot of the season. They are not the WNBA's official league awards, which are announced separately. That distinction belongs in the first paragraph, not in fine print after the confetti.

The 2026 ballot is unusually good at showing both kinds of greatness an award list can capture. Wilson added another layer to a career that already owns plenty of hardware. Reese, Miles, Clark, Shepard and Salaün each won their category for the first time. Reeve did both at once: another trophy, but a new kind of season to explain it.

sections.title: A'ja did not just win. She moved the record
paragraphs: Wilson received 15 of the 17 first-place votes, and the number that matters most is four. Her AP Player of the Year wins now span 2020, 2024, 2025 and 2026. Breanna Stewart had been the only three-time winner. Wilson did not join her; she stepped past her.

The vote reads like a reward for total control. Wilson led the league in scoring at 26.2 points per game, made nearly 53 percent of her shots, pulled down 9.4 rebounds and blocked 1.9 shots. The 3.2 assists were a career best. That last number is the quiet one: the best scorer on the floor kept improving the decisions that happen after the second defender arrives.

sections.title: Reese won the argument at the end of possessions
paragraphs: The defensive award had belonged to Wilson in three of the previous four AP seasons. Reese broke that grip with a case built on volume, activity and possession control. She led the league in rebounding for the third straight year, finished the regular season with 521 boards and placed third in steals.

Rebounding is not every part of defense, but ending the possession is not a decorative skill. Reese's best argument was how often Atlanta got to stop playing defense once she entered the play. Her hands created turnovers, her range let the Dream move her through coverages, and her work on the glass kept opponents from turning one good action into two shots.

sections.title: Miles and Clark tell two different return stories
paragraphs: Miles was the unanimous rookie choice because she never looked like she was waiting for the game to slow down. She averaged 19.8 points and 6.0 assists, set the league's rookie scoring record and operated the offense for the No. 1 seed. The history tab makes the larger point: AP Rookie of the Year has produced a different winner in all 11 seasons, and Miles belongs to a line that runs from Breanna Stewart to Caitlin Clark to Paige Bueckers.

Clark's Comeback Player award is about availability as much as stardom. After injuries limited her in 2025, she played 40 games, averaged 22.3 points and 8.3 assists, and restored Indiana's ability to stretch a defense until it snapped. The comeback category has never repeated a winner. That is fitting: its value is in the specific road back, not a permanent tier of player.

sections.title: Shepard and Salaün stretched their job descriptions
paragraphs: Most Improved is sometimes treated like a scoring-jump prize. Shepard made a more interesting case. She averaged 14.5 points, 11.1 rebounds and 5.3 assists and recorded six triple-doubles. Dallas gave her more minutes, but the real leap was the number of possessions she could organize from the frontcourt.

Salaün's sixth-woman case was cleaner and louder. She came off Golden State's bench in all 40 games and led every reserve with 509 points. Her 93 made threes were a reserve record, and she shot 39.2 percent from deep. A bench label usually describes when someone checks in. Salaün made it describe how quickly the geometry changed.

sections.title: Reeve's third trophy was a systems award
paragraphs: Minnesota reached the top seed even though Napheesa Collier missed the first half of the season. Reeve had to build one version of the Lynx without the franchise star, then make room for Collier without asking everyone else to forget what had worked. That is not simply surviving an absence. It is designing a team that can absorb a superstar and remain itself.

The win gives Reeve three AP Coach of the Year awards, one more than Curt Miller. Her 2020, 2024 and 2026 trophies also describe three different coaching problems, which is the strongest part of the record.

sections.title: The history dashboard tells on the ballot
paragraphs: Some awards build dynasties. Wilson and Stewart have won seven of the 11 Player of the Year votes. Wilson and Sylvia Fowles account for six of the 11 defensive trophies. Reeve and Miller own five Coach of the Year wins between them.

Other categories resist a repeat. Rookie and Most Improved are 11-for-11 on unique winners. Comeback has 12 recipients because Collier and Brittney Griner shared the 2023 honor, and none has repeated. Sixth Woman sits between those worlds: Dearica Hamby is the only two-time winner. The interactive history is useful because it makes those category personalities visible without pretending every award measures greatness the same way.

sections.title: The AP teams are an honor roll, not a lineup card
paragraphs: Wilson, Clark, Miles, Kelsey Mitchell and Stewart made the first team. Reese, Rhyne Howard, Paige Bueckers, Jackie Young and Gabby Williams made the second. The selections reward the season's best work; they are not a promise that the five names fit neatly into traditional positions.

The six-player All-Rookie team came from a ballot tie: Miles, Azzi Fudd, Sydney Taylor, Flau'jae Johnson, Pauline Astier and Kiki Rice. It is a good problem for an awards list to have. The 2026 class did not need the ballot to shrink so its impact would look tidy.

sections.title: The WNBA’s All-Defensive First Team is a separate honor
paragraphs: Update · Oct. 15, 2026: The WNBA’s official All-Defensive First Team is Shakira Austin of the Washington Mystics, Rhyne Howard and Angel Reese of the Atlanta Dream, Gabby Williams of the Golden State Valkyries, and A’ja Wilson of the Las Vegas Aces. This is the league’s team selection; the awards and All-AP teams above are Associated Press honors.

Reese’s first Kia Defensive Player of the Year award adds context to her First Team selection. She received 46 votes from the 74-member national panel, ahead of Williams (20) and Wilson (4). Reese also led the league with 12.1 rebounds per game and set single-season records with 521 total rebounds and 206 offensive rebounds. Atlanta finished third in defensive rating at 103.5.

The overlap is striking: all four leading finishers in the league’s Defensive Player of the Year vote—Reese, Williams, Wilson and Austin—made this First Team, and Howard joined them. Atlanta is the only team with two selections. The official league team and the AP ballot remain distinct honors.

foodSegment.title: Read the list twice
foodSegment.script: The first read is for the winners. The second is for the shape of the league: Wilson's sustained peak, Reese's possession-ending defense, Miles running a contender immediately, Clark getting a healthy season back, and role players whose roles stopped fitting in one sentence. That second read is where an award list becomes a season story.

sections.title: East: Angel Reese made it three straight
paragraphs: Reese was named Eastern Conference Player of the Week for the third consecutive time, becoming the first player in Atlanta Dream history to win the honor three weeks in a row. Atlanta went 4-0 in the final week, and Reese averaged 19.3 points, 9.0 rebounds, 3.0 assists, 1.3 steals and 1.5 blocks while shooting 60.4 percent from the field.

The award is the fifth weekly honor of Reese's WNBA career. She was also named a WNBA Peak Performer after leading the league at 12.3 rebounds per game, and she became the first WNBA player to reach 500 rebounds in a single season.

sections.title: Game 4: Golden State answers in Atlanta
paragraphs: Golden State beat Atlanta 67–62 at State Farm Arena on October 24, leveling the best-of-seven Finals at 2–2. Gabby Williams scored 17, Rhyne Howard led Atlanta with 19, and the Dream was held to 33.3 percent shooting.

Atlanta made the ending tense: Howard’s three-point play with 28 seconds left cut the margin to four. Golden State answered at the line, then Atlanta missed its final two three-point attempts. Tiffany Hayes scored all 13 of her points after halftime; Kiah Stokes pulled down 16 rebounds, including eight on the offensive glass.

sections.title: The turnover swing changed the possession math
paragraphs: Atlanta won the rebound count 51–42, but Golden State won the turnover battle 9–18 and scored 16 points off those mistakes to Atlanta’s eight. That eight-point edge in turnover scoring was larger than the five-point final margin. The takeaway: Atlanta created more total possessions; Golden State got more immediate value from the giveaways.

There was a second lever. Golden State grabbed 13 offensive rebounds to Atlanta’s 12, with Stokes collecting eight of them. Atlanta still edged second-chance points 8–5, so the extra boards did not become a scoring advantage by themselves. They kept the Valkyries’ offense alive while its shots were not falling: Golden State made 36.1 percent from the field and 16 percent from three.

sections.title: Game 3: dreams to nightmares in Atlanta
paragraphs: Atlanta beat Golden State 97–71 at State Farm Arena on October 21. The Dream led 23–15 after one quarter and 46–40 at halftime, then answered Golden State’s third-quarter push with an 8–0 run over the final 2:11. Atlanta closed with a 26–14 fourth quarter, turning a competitive middle stretch into the largest win of the series.

Angel Reese finished with 21 points, 12 rebounds, three assists and two steals, recording a double-double in each of her first three Finals games. Rhyne Howard added 16 points, five steals and four assists; Naz Hillmon scored 15. The final official box score lists Howard at 16, resolving an early live-blog line that reported 18.

Golden State got 15 points from Gabby Williams, 14 from Tiffany Hayes and 13 apiece from Cecilia Zandalasini and Janelle Salaün. Kiah Stokes blocked four shots. The Valkyries’ bench won 38–27, but Atlanta’s starting group supplied 70 points and controlled the decisive stretches.

sections.title: The possession math behind the 26-point gap
paragraphs: Atlanta shot 34-for-69 from the floor (49.3 percent) and 9-for-22 from three (40.9 percent). Golden State finished 24-for-69 (34.8 percent) and 12-for-30 from three (40.0 percent). The Valkyries matched Atlanta’s perimeter accuracy, but Atlanta made 22 two-point baskets to Golden State’s 12 and won the paint 44–20.

The free-throw margin mattered without carrying the whole result: Atlanta went 20-for-29, Golden State 11-for-17. Ball security created the sharper divide. The Dream committed 10 total turnovers and scored 22 points off Golden State’s 17; the Valkyries scored seven points off Atlanta’s miscues. Atlanta also assisted on 26 of 34 field goals.

Golden State owned the offensive glass 9–6, second-chance scoring 10–4 and bench scoring 38–27. Atlanta still won total rebounds 51–44 because it finished possessions with 31 defensive rebounds and kept converting stops into organized offense. Those counters explain why the visitors’ useful advantages never became scoreboard pressure.

sections.title: What Game 5 asks from both sides
paragraphs: Atlanta’s clearest adjustment is to protect the ball while keeping its rebounding edge useful. The Dream turned it over 18 times in Game 4, and the Valkyries made those mistakes cost points. Golden State’s challenge is to preserve that defensive pressure without relying on a 16-point halftime lead to survive another Atlanta rally.

The series returns to Chase Center tied 2–2. Game 5 is Monday, October 26, at 8 p.m. ET on USA and Peacock. The team that wins takes a 3–2 lead; Game 6 in Atlanta and Game 7 in San Francisco are scheduled only if needed.

sections.title: Game 2: Atlanta answers at Chase Center
paragraphs: Atlanta won 79–65 on October 19, earning its first Finals victory and evening the series. The third quarter delivered the decisive separation: Atlanta 21, Golden State 9. A two-point halftime gap became 14 entering the fourth, and the teams traded 19 points apiece from there.

Angel Reese finished with 30 points, 16 rebounds and three assists. Allisha Gray supplied 18 points; Jordin Canada paired 13 points with 10 assists and seven rebounds. Rhyne Howard scored only five, but her six steals show why scoring alone misses Atlanta’s most disruptive work.

Golden State had 14 points from Gabby Williams, 11 rebounds and four blocks from Kiah Stokes, and three made threes from Kaila Charles. The bench outscored Atlanta 33–11. Veronica Burton added 11 points. That depth kept producing, but the starters combined for only 32 points.

sections.title: Game 1: Williams finishes the job
paragraphs: Golden State won 68–64 on October 17. Atlanta led 22–14 after one quarter; Golden State answered 28–17 in the second. Atlanta regained a 56–51 edge entering the fourth before the Valkyries won that period 17–8.

Gabby Williams supplied 26 points, including 16 in the second quarter, a total the official team recap places tied third in Finals quarter history. Golden State scored the final seven points, with Williams making six free throws. Kiah Stokes added nine points, seven rebounds and four blocks.

The support came through possession work: Kaila Charles had 10 rebounds, Tiffany Hayes six rebounds and four assists, and Laeticia Amihere five points and five rebounds. Golden State won player rebounds 41–35 and bench scoring 20–6. Its 17 points off turnovers more than doubled Atlanta’s eight.

Allisha Gray scored 19, Angel Reese 14 with 12 rebounds, and Rhyne Howard 12. Gray and Howard combined to shoot 8-for-33. Golden State survived limited scoring breadth by extending possessions, protecting the rim and closing with Williams. Atlanta’s response came two days later.

sections.title: Game 2: the arithmetic behind Atlanta’s answer
paragraphs: Both teams made 21 field goals and seven three-pointers. Atlanta’s 14-point winning margin therefore matches its advantage at the free-throw line exactly: 30 makes to Golden State’s 16. The Dream attempted 35 free throws; the Valkyries attempted 19. Those totals describe the difference in the box score; they do not establish whether any particular whistle was correct.

Atlanta also won the possession exchanges. Golden State committed 19 turnovers to Atlanta’s 14, while the Dream scored 24 points off turnovers against 13 for the Valkyries. Atlanta’s 17–7 edge in second-chance points added another route to scoring without needing a better shooting percentage.

Analysis: a nearly identical field-goal output can disguise very different offensive nights. Atlanta generated enough trips to the line and extra-possession scoring to win comfortably despite shooting 33.9 percent from the floor. Golden State’s 34.4 percent was scarcely better; the ball security and foul-line gaps made that shared struggle much more expensive for the home side.

sections.title: Atlanta gets the last possession right
paragraphs: The Dream beat New York 85–83 on October 9 and swept the semifinals 3–0. DeWanna Bonner secured the late rebound and made both free throws; Breanna Stewart’s final putback could only trim the margin.
Angel Reese supplied 22 points and nine rebounds, Rhyne Howard scored 21 and Jordin Canada paired 19 with 11 assists. Bonner added 13 points and 13 boards; Isobel Borlase scored 10 off the bench.
Atlanta returns to the Finals for the first time since 2013. Its next test is Golden State’s defensive pressure and depth.

sections.title: The Valkyries turn five extra minutes into a ticket
paragraphs: Golden State finished Las Vegas 87–77 in overtime, completing a 3–0 sweep. A 17–0 third-quarter run changed the game; an 8–0 fourth-quarter burst helped force the extra period.
The Valkyries won overtime 16–6. Kayla Thornton scored 18, Gabby Williams 16, and Tiffany Hayes and Kiah Stokes 11 each. Stokes went 5-for-5 and recorded a double-double.
Hayes passed 500 career playoff points. Golden State reaches its first Finals in its second season, with home court against Atlanta.

sections.title: Two exits change the talent audit
paragraphs: New York and Las Vegas are eliminated. Their draft pedigrees remain part of the semifinal story, but no longer count toward the players still chasing this title.
The two finalists have 11 top-10 picks between them: seven for Atlanta and four for Golden State. Rhyne Howard is the lone No. 1 pick among those two rosters.
Analysis: premium picks can supply options, but depth, defensive coordination and late-possession execution decide whether those options survive a series.

sections.title: A first title is guaranteed
paragraphs: Atlanta and Golden State are each chasing the first WNBA championship in franchise history.
The No. 2 seed Valkyries and No. 4 seed Dream have reached a best-of-seven Finals after taking different routes through the postseason.

sections.title: Renee Montgomery’s story has two Finals seats
paragraphs: Dream partner and vice president Renee Montgomery won WNBA championships with Minnesota in 2015 and 2017. She joined Atlanta’s ownership group in 2021; when the Dream clinched a 2026 Finals berth, she became the first person in WNBA history to reach the Finals as both a player and team owner.

The WNBA describes Montgomery as the first former player to hold both team equity and an executive title. Her Finals story now spans two franchises and two roles: champion on the floor, then a Finals-bound owner in Atlanta.

awardFallout.dek: Minnesota entered with the league’s top seed, the Coach of the Year and the unanimous Rookie of the Year. Two 16-point losses ended that season before October.

people.name: Cheryl Reeve
people.playoff: New York’s size, switching and half-court execution won both games. Because Reeve also leads basketball operations, the exit puts the adjustment plan and roster construction under the same spotlight.

people.name: Olivia Miles
people.playoff: New York compressed her driving and passing windows. Miles averaged 8.0 points and 5.0 assists in the series, shot 20 percent and was replaced late in Game 2 — a harsh first lesson, not a rewrite of her rookie season.

implications.title: Awards measure months, not two nights
implications.text: Reeve’s 33-win season and Miles’ record-setting rookie résumé remain the right evidence for regular-season awards. A playoff loss does not retroactively change those ballots.

implications.title: The format debate gets louder
implications.text: A best-of-three makes matchup variance and one bad adjustment enormous. The result strengthens the case for a best-of-five first round, even though New York’s two 16-point wins were emphatic rather than fluky.

implications.title: Postseason scouting found the pressure point
implications.text: The Liberty made Miles play through length and reduced Minnesota’s easy creation. Her response next season will matter more than the fact that an elite defense solved a rookie once.

implications.title: Minnesota’s standard changes the review
implications.text: Coach of the Year confirms Reeve built the league’s best regular-season team. The sweep means the offseason review has to ask why that team could not produce a workable counter before the series ended.

awardFallout.verdict: The trophy case says who sustained excellence over 44 games. The bracket asks who can solve this opponent right now. Minnesota won the first argument; New York won the one that keeps the season alive.

posts.seriesLabel: FOOD FOR THOUGHT · CONNECTICUT SUN FAREWELL
posts.title: One Last Sunrise: Farewell to the Connecticut Sun
posts.imageAlt: Connecticut Sun fans celebrate the franchise at its final home game in Mohegan Sun Arena
posts.dek: The final record was 11–33. The final result was a win. Between those two facts sits 24 seasons of Connecticut basketball that deserve to be remembered.

sections.title: A final night worth keeping
paragraphs: Connecticut beat Toronto 95–81 at Mohegan Sun Arena on Sept. 24, 2026. The Sun ended their last season 11–33, with a one-game winning streak. A hard year did not get the last word: the players and crowd got one more win together.
The team is moving to Houston and will be renamed the Comets in 2027. Connecticut fans have every right to hold on to what was built in Uncasville.

sections.title: 2003: a home by the river
paragraphs: After the Orlando Miracle relocated, the Mohegan Tribe brought the franchise to Connecticut in 2003. Playing at Mohegan Sun Arena made the Sun a place people traveled to, returned to and claimed as their own. The Tribe’s ownership was a defining part of the identity.

sections.title: 2004 and 2005: the first close calls
paragraphs: Mike Thibault’s early Sun reached back-to-back WNBA Finals. Seattle won in 2004; Sacramento won in 2005. Lindsay Whalen, Nykesha Sales and Asjha Jones helped set a standard: Connecticut could meet the league’s best on the biggest stage.

sections.title: 2019 and 2022: the door stayed open
paragraphs: The 2019 Sun took Washington to a deciding fifth game in the Finals. In 2022, behind a bruising frontcourt featuring Alyssa Thomas, DeWanna Bonner, Brionna Jones and Jonquel Jones, Connecticut made its fourth Finals appearance. Different faces, familiar promise: the Sun were never easy to put away.

sections.title: The people who gave the jersey its weight
paragraphs: Jonquel Jones won the 2021 MVP award as a Sun and had her No. 35 honored at the arena in 2026. Alyssa Thomas turned versatility and toughness into a team language. Across eras, players, coaches, staff and supporters made Connecticut a fixture in the postseason conversation.
No championship banner arrived. Four Finals trips did, and so did the habit of believing the next one could be different. That is a legacy bigger than one difficult final standings line.

sections.title: One game, one streak, decades of light
paragraphs: The final box score reads Sun 95, Tempo 81. It cannot show every seat filled across 24 seasons, or every player who grew into herself in this building. The name leaves the schedule. The memories, and the people who made them, stay in Connecticut.

posts.title: The Fever Got the Bench. What Did Minnesota Actually Give Away?
posts.imageAlt: Minnesota Lynx players gather during a game
posts.storyImageCaption: Minnesota Lynx game photography, via the official September 22 game preview.
posts.dek: Indiana needed the win. Minnesota needed to get healthy. By halftime, those priorities were obvious. The Fever took the 96-77 win, but the second half became something else: a live playoff-depth test.

rankings.note: The deepest playoff bench by a mile. Janelle Salaun is a Sixth Player favorite, Tiffany Hayes brings another veteran creator, and Golden State can change lineups without changing its identity.
Marine Johannes gives New York instant offense and movement. The Liberty second unit is efficient enough to survive short starter rests without asking one player to do everything.
Dallas gets useful scoring and activity from its reserves. The question is how much of that survives when playoff rotations shrink.
Jewell Loyd gives Vegas something most benches do not have: a former All-Star who can still take over possessions. The Aces do not need huge bench minutes, just dependable ones.
Sophie Cunningham keeps pace and spacing around the stars. Indiana's bench is not the headline, but it can keep the offense from falling off a cliff.
Young, physical and willing to defend. Washington's depth matters because the Mystics can keep size on the floor when the starters sit.
Atlanta leans harder on its starting group. The bench has been efficient, but the playoff question is whether it can buy enough clean minutes for the stars.
Lowest regular-season bench scoring among the playoff field, but Tuesday showed why raw bench PPG can lie. Minnesota's reserves cut a 29-point hole to eight before Indiana's starters closed it out.

sections.title: Did Minnesota prioritize rest?
paragraphs: Not from the opening tip. Olivia Miles was already out with a calf injury, but Minnesota started Napheesa Collier, Kayla McBride, Courtney Williams and the rest of its available first unit. Indiana then punched them in the mouth. The Fever led 31-16 after one quarter and pushed the margin to 29 in the first half.

That is when Cheryl Reeve changed the assignment. She sat her starters for most of the final two and a half quarters because she did not want to risk another injury. So yes, rest and health became the priority, but only after Indiana had already taken control. Calling the entire win gift wrapped lets Minnesota's starters off too easily.

sections.title: Still, Indiana got a very nice gift
paragraphs: Indiana needed this one to keep its home-court hopes alive. Instead of spending 40 minutes dealing with Minnesota's best five, the Fever spent most of the second half playing the Lynx reserves.

The funny part is that the bench made Indiana work. Chloe Bibby hit five threes and scored 15. Liatu King had 12 points, four rebounds and three steals. Aari McDonald added 10 points and five assists. Minnesota cut a 29-point deficit to eight before Caitlin Clark, Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston finally shut the door.

sections.title: That is the part Minnesota should keep
paragraphs: The loss matters because the No. 1 seed still is not clinched. The way the bench responded matters for a different reason. Playoff benches are not supposed to win four-minute stretches by accident. They have to survive foul trouble, injuries and the ugly minutes when a starter needs air.

Minnesota ranks last among the eight playoff teams in regular-season bench scoring. Tuesday did not magically make the Lynx the deepest team in the field. It did show that their reserves can defend, run and drag a game back into range when the stars are sitting.

sections.title: Golden State has the bench everybody else has to answer
paragraphs: Golden State is in its own category. The Valkyries are around 36 bench points per game, roughly 13 more than the next playoff team. Janelle Salaun has 492 points off the bench, the most in the league, while shooting 39.7 percent from three.

That depth already mattered after Berlin. With several World Cup players resting, Golden State still beat Portland 82-66 behind Laeticia Amihere and Kaitlyn Chen. That is not emergency depth. That is part of the system.

sections.title: The Sixth Woman board
paragraphs: Salaun is the standard here. ESPN's four-person awards panel unanimously picked her for Sixth Player of the Year, and the production backs up the attention. Marine Johannes gives New York a different kind of weapon, Sophie Cunningham keeps Indiana's second unit connected to its spacing, and Jewell Loyd gives Las Vegas a scorer with starter-level experience.

The playoffs will shrink rotations, but that makes these players more important, not less. The question is not who has ten playable bodies. It is who has a sixth and seventh player a coach actually trusts when the game gets tight.

sections.title: Shak's read
paragraphs: Indiana earned the lead. Minnesota chose not to chase it with its starters. Both things can be true.

The Fever got exactly what they needed: a win without having to beat Minnesota's best lineup for four quarters. The Lynx got something too: a long look at the players who may have to save a playoff possession, a quarter or a game when the plan goes sideways.
Thursday's rematch is the one that tells us more. If Minnesota brings the full group and treats it like a playoff tune-up, then we finally get the matchup Tuesday was supposed to be.

posts.title: The Seats Are Moving
posts.dek: Everybody already has a playoff ticket. Now the seats are moving. Atlanta took another step toward home court, New York is officially opening on the road, and Dallas finally got clipped after six straight wins.

sections.title: Atlanta keeps handling business
paragraphs: Atlanta came back from Berlin and apparently decided losing could wait. The Dream beat New York 95-84 on Monday and moved to 29-14.
That makes three straight wins since the break. One more win over New York on Wednesday, or one Indiana loss, locks up first-round home court for Atlanta.

sections.title: New York, pack a road bag
paragraphs: The Liberty had a nice little run going. They beat Minnesota, put 106 on Toronto and came home with a chance to keep pushing up the bracket.
Atlanta ended that. New York is 26-17 now, and first-round home court is officially gone. The Liberty are in. They are just starting the playoffs in somebody else's building.

sections.title: Dallas finally blinked
paragraphs: Dallas won six straight and made the bottom of the bracket a whole lot more interesting. Then Phoenix stole one by a point.
Kahleah Copper's layup with two seconds left gave the Mercury an 87-86 win. Paige Bueckers had 30 points and seven assists, but the last shot did not fall. Dallas is 26-17 with one game left.

sections.title: Shak's bite
paragraphs: Everybody has a ticket. Nobody has the same seat they thought they had a few days ago.

Atlanta is trying to keep home court. New York knows it is traveling. Dallas just lost its six-game heater. Minnesota still has Golden State behind it, and Vegas is sitting right in the middle of the top-four mess.
Two days left. Keep the bracket in pencil.
